Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation; repeated sampling cannot remove this discrepancy. Smaller candidate sets weaken emphasis on top ranks. They recommend full-catalog evaluation where feasible and propose corrections when sampling is necessary. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation, KDD 2020](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

Exact conditional derivation: let N≥99 be the eligible competitors excluding the target, with g strictly higher scores, e equal scores, and N−g−e lower scores. Drawing 99 unique negatives uniformly without replacement gives sampled higher/tied counts (A,B) with probability P(A=a,B=b)=C(g,a)C(e,b)C(N−g−e,99−a−b)/C(N,99). Given these counts, uniform tie breaking places the target uniformly at ranks a+1,…,a+b+1, so its hit probability is h(a,b)=min(1,max(0,(10−a)/(b+1))). Therefore E[HR@10 | scores]=ΣₐΣᵦ P(A=a,B=b)h(a,b), summing feasible counts. Without ties this reduces to the hypergeometric CDF P(A≤9).

The corresponding full-catalog expectation is min(1,max(0,(10−g)/(e+1))). Subtracting it from the sampled expectation isolates the discrepancy caused by candidate sampling under these assumptions. Average per-user expectations within each category, then average the four category means. This replaces five-draw Monte Carlo estimates with an exact conditional reference, without changing the pinned evaluator. It removes candidate-sampling and tie-breaking simulation noise, not uncertainty from user selection or training. Counts must use the evaluator’s eligible negative pool; uniform tie breaking must match its actual behavior.
